question: I play Death Mark from my trash for its Flow cost. My opponent counters it with Defy. Death Mark's Flow cost is [1][A][A], which is more Power than Defy allows — can Defy even target it? And if it resolves, does Death Mark go to my trash (so I could Flow it again) or is it banished?
reframe: two questions: does Defy's cost restriction read Death Mark's base cost or the Flow cost actually paid, and does Counter's "placed in the trash" or Flow's delayed banish win when a Flow spell is cleared from the chain?

holding.line: Yes, Defy can counter it — cost restrictions read the base cost, not the Flow cost you paid — and Death Mark is then banished rather than trashed, so you cannot Flow it a second time.

spans.text: cost restrictions read the base cost, not the Flow cost you paid
you cannot Flow it a second time

notes.claim: Defy's restriction is measured against Death Mark's printed cost of 2 Energy and 1 Power, which is within both limits.
notes.detail: Defy counters "a spell that costs no more than [4] and no more than [A]". Death Mark is printed at 2 Energy / 1 Power. Its Flow cost of [1][A][A] is louder but irrelevant — see n2.

cites.quote: Effects that need to determine an ability’s cost for any purpose use its base cost, ignoring any alterations to that base cost unless otherwise specified.

notes.claim: A Flow cost is an alternate cost, so it is an alteration rather than the spell's cost.
notes.detail: This is the crux of the first half: read the Flow cost instead and Death Mark's 2 Power exceeds Defy's [A] limit, making the counter illegal.

cites.quote: The cost is an alternate cost that replaces the base cost of the spell to be paid during finalization.

notes.claim: Countering clears the spell from the chain and would put it in the trash.

cites.quote: A card or ability that is Countered does nothing and is cleared from the chain.
Cards that are cleared from the chain in this way are placed in the trash.

notes.claim: Flow's banish is a delayed replacement effect, so it replaces that trip to the trash.
notes.detail: Death Mark became a finalized chain item when it was played, and Counter — not Death Mark's own execution — is what removes it. Both conditions in 829.1.b.1 are met, so "banish it instead" replaces 425.1.a.1's trash placement. No single rule states the outcome for a countered Flow spell; it follows from the replacement applying to this exact departure.
notes.if_false: If the banish only applied to a spell that resolves, a countered Death Mark would sit in the trash and could be Flowed again on a later turn. The first half of the answer is unaffected either way.

cites.quote: If the spell would leave the chain after becoming a finalized chain item, and leaving the chain wasn’t instructed by its own execution, banish it instead.

notes.claim: A banished Death Mark is out of reach of Flow, which only ever plays from the trash.

cites.quote: It is functionally short for “You may play this from your trash for its flow cost. Then banish it.”

counterargument.reading: The banish is part of "Then banish it" in Flow's own wording, so it only happens after the spell successfully resolves. A countered spell never resolves, so it just goes to the trash like any other countered card.
counterargument.why_it_loses: 829.1.b.1 exists precisely to say that this is not sequencing but a delayed replacement, and it is written around the spell leaving the chain rather than around it resolving. Being countered is a departure from the chain that Death Mark's own execution did not instruct, which is the case the rule describes.

cites.quote: Banishing the spell in this way is a delayed replacement effect.

considered_rejected.why: Confirms the Flow cost is not refunded, but says nothing about where the card ends up.
